frictionVectors.title: European energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons, but European demand and pipeline diplomacy create pressure over pricing, supply reliability, and investment terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign technology dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil and gas production remains nationally controlled, although advanced extraction, LNG, and renewable technologies still rely partly on external partners.

highlights: Oil revenue still anchors the state

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Angola is pursuing diversification and local-content reforms, but declining or volatile oil output continues to constrain fiscal sovereignty and economic resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese financing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-built infrastructure remains strategically important, while debt-servicing obligations and external contractors limit Luanda's flexibility over major transport and energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insecurity spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens roads, agricultural production, and state access to northern resources, increasing reliance on external security support.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's logistics role is strategically valuable, but trade restrictions, regional political tensions, and foreign investment in transport infrastructure can dilute national control over key corridors.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its share of diamond value and marketing influence, but continued dependence on De Beers-linked expertise and global distribution remains a strategic vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective copper, nickel, and battery-mineral projects attract external capital, creating a manageable tension between rapid development and maintaining strict national oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector restructuring
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater state participation and tighter control over gold production, but informal mining, smuggling, and contested territory weaken effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: External security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from Western military partners toward Russian-linked support has increased geopolitical autonomy rhetoric, while insecurity continues to threaten roads, mines, and energy infrastructure.

highlights: Nickel and rare-earth ambitions remain state-controlled but underfunded
Regional diplomacy is constrained by Rwanda tensions

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Burundi Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and cross-border support continue to restrict trade and regional coordination. The dispute also complicates transport links to ports and mineral markets.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi seeks foreign capital and technology to develop nickel and rare-earth deposits, giving external investors leverage over licensing, infrastructure, and future export revenues.

highlights: Atlantic logistics and maritime security raise strategic value
Diversified partnerships preserve relatively strong policy autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: The government is balancing European, American, Chinese, and private-sector interest in ports, digital infrastructure, and maritime services. Dependence on external finance could narrow bargaining room if projects underperform.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Desalination, renewable-energy, and grid expansion remain reliant on imported equipment and concessional funding. Climate stress and high logistics costs continue to constrain sovereign resource security.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and mining remain exposed to external operators
Infrastructure diplomacy is increasingly shaped by China and Gulf-linked capital

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Corridor Risk
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest regions threatens roads, plantations, and energy infrastructure. Prolonged insecurity weakens central control over productive assets and raises the cost of national integration.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and foreign investors remain important in roads, ports, rail, and resource projects. Debt, opaque contracting, and limited domestic processing reduce the state’s ability to capture full value.

highlights: Security partnerships with Russia have displaced much Western leverage
Mining sovereignty remains limited by insecurity and opaque concessions

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security actors provide regime protection while retaining influence around gold and diamond production. This arrangement strengthens short-term state survival but risks transferring resource rents outside accountable institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Trade Routes
frictionVectors.details: Militias and rebel factions continue to affect access to mining areas, border crossings, and agricultural corridors. Regional instability limits customs collection and makes infrastructure investment highly vulnerable.

highlights: Oil remains the fiscal anchor and principal source of external leverage
Sudan spillover is reshaping border security and humanitarian priorities

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s budget and foreign-exchange position remain heavily dependent on hydrocarbons transported through regional infrastructure. External operators, transit arrangements, and volatile prices constrain sovereign control over revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War and Sahel Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in Sudan is driving refugee flows, arms movement, and cross-border insecurity. Competing foreign security and financial partners gain leverage as N'Djamena prioritizes regime stability and border control.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the main sovereignty dispute, constraining Comoros' control over surrounding maritime space and migration policy.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic capacity and reliance on remittances, foreign aid, and imported fuel leave strategic infrastructure and resource development vulnerable to outside influence.

frictionVectors.title: Minerals and Contract Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains heavily shaped by foreign capital and opaque or politically contested contracts, limiting the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: M23's territorial challenge, attributed by Kinshasa to Rwanda, continues to weaken state control in the east and intensify competition over trade corridors and mineral zones.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked oil production and volatile petroleum revenues constrain fiscal autonomy and leave the state exposed to external market and financing pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port projects provide strategic connectivity but deepen concerns over debt, project transparency, and long-term control of logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Dependence and Foreign Processing
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire is expanding local processing and state oversight, but foreign firms still dominate financing, trading, and higher-value segments of the cocoa chain.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability from Burkina Faso and Mali continues to pressure northern borders and security spending while increasing the strategic importance of Abidjan's transport and port infrastructure.

highlights: Bases and Ports Drive Strategic Leverage

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Competing US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and deterrence but make Djibouti's sovereignty dependent on rival external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port and rail financing has strengthened Djibouti's logistics role while creating persistent concerns over debt sustainability and foreign influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and Gulf investment provide vital liquidity but constrain policy autonomy and increase foreign influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea threaten Suez revenues, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains a core sovereignty and water-security concern.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling oil output and limited diversification weaken state revenues, increasing reliance on foreign operators and external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and construction exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked infrastructure and offshore energy partnerships remain central to connectivity, but may deepen debt, transparency, and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mining partner concentration
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard-currency earnings, but dependence on a narrow group of foreign operators leaves leverage over contracts and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia, Sudan, and Red Sea actors keep ports and border corridors exposed to outside security competition.

frictionVectors.title: Single-market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, fuel, and logistics remain heavily tied to South Africa, limiting Eswatini's room for independent resource and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Revenue-transfer vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on regional customs revenues and foreign-owned manufacturing makes fiscal stability sensitive to Southern African trade and investment shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water dispute
frictionVectors.details: The GERD strengthens Ethiopia's control over its power system, but unresolved operating arrangements with Egypt and Sudan remain a major diplomatic flashpoint.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and logistics
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, Chinese exposure, and reliance on Djibouti corridors constrain economic sovereignty while conflict-related instability raises infrastructure risks.

frictionVectors.title: French influence recalibration
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is renegotiating long-standing French security, commercial, and infrastructure ties while seeking broader partnerships. The transition has reduced some external dependence but created uncertainty for established investors.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil, manganese, and timber remain dominated by large foreign-linked operators, limiting domestic value capture. Authorities are pushing local processing and tighter contract oversight without yet having the capacity to replace external expertise.

highlights: Ports and tourism remain externally dependent

frictionVectors.title: Senegal border and maritime exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's economy and security remain closely tied to Senegal, including transport corridors and regional military cooperation. Disputes over fishing access and border commerce can quickly affect food and revenue security.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-funded infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, energy, and tourism projects rely heavily on European, Gulf, Chinese, and multilateral financing. This expands connectivity but leaves limited fiscal space for fully sovereign infrastructure planning.

highlights: Gold and critical minerals strategy hardens

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and informal mining is damaging water, farmland, and state legitimacy while gold revenues leak through opaque trading networks. The government is trying to formalize purchasing and increase domestic refining, but enforcement remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization under the IMF program and debt restructuring restricts spending choices and the state's ability to subsidize strategic infrastructure. Ghana is seeking greater local participation in lithium, bauxite, and manganese while remaining dependent on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore complex and associated rail and port infrastructure are being developed through foreign-led consortia, especially Chinese-linked interests. The projects offer transformative revenue but risk locking Guinea into enclave logistics and uneven benefit sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Civilian transition and contract risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining renegotiations and local-content demands to strengthen state control while delaying or tightly managing political liberalization. Investor uncertainty and sanctions exposure could weaken oversight and deepen dependence on a narrow group of external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and public revenues vulnerable to foreign buyers, price swings, and port disruptions. India and other external markets exert substantial influence over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine trafficking and political capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement make the country vulnerable to transshipment networks linking Latin America and Europe. Trafficking revenues can distort security-sector politics and undermine sovereign control of ports and borders.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and reliance on multilateral financing limit Nairobi's policy autonomy. Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders compete for influence over infrastructure and fiscal priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the Lamu corridor remain exposed to competition from regional ports and external investors. Control of logistics, rail, and energy infrastructure remains a central sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria for financing, infrastructure, and market access. Delays and cost disputes can quickly become political flashpoints.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and Mining Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned textile production and diamond mining generate employment but leave value chains and export earnings vulnerable to external market decisions. Limited economic diversification weakens domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital and require concessions, roads, and port access. The government faces pressure to improve revenue capture without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and Liberia's major maritime registry attract international commercial influence. Weak domestic logistics capacity limits Liberia's ability to convert strategic access into broader sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed factions continue to contest control of oil fields, export terminals, and state institutions. Foreign powers and energy firms retain leverage through security partnerships, contracts, and diplomatic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port and Border Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mediterranean ports, southern transit routes, and migration corridors are exposed to rival external security agendas. Infrastructure remains vulnerable to blockades, militia coercion, and opaque foreign contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects are driven by foreign capital and export demand, while Madagascar retains limited processing capacity and bargaining power. Commodity-price swings and infrastructure bottlenecks constrain sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit Natural Resource Networks
frictionVectors.details: Illegal rosewood, gemstones, and fisheries trafficking continue to erode state control in remote regions. External buyers and weak enforcement make resource governance vulnerable to transnational networks.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Conditional Finance
frictionVectors.details: Malawi remains dependent on IMF, World Bank, and bilateral restructuring support, limiting policy autonomy while restoring macroeconomic stability. Debt-service pressures constrain public investment in energy, transport, and food security.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare earths, and niobium is growing, but weak electricity and transport infrastructure reduce Malawi's bargaining power. The government is seeking greater local value addition without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: State Pressure on Foreign Miners
frictionVectors.details: The junta is demanding larger state and local shares of gold production, creating recurring disputes with international mining companies. Revenue gains are offset by operational uncertainty, sanctions exposure, and weak regulatory capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security support has reduced Western influence but increased dependence on a new external patron. Persistent militant violence threatens mining corridors, agricultural supply routes, and state control beyond major cities.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Revenue Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens Mauritania's fiscal and diplomatic leverage, but offshore gas revenue management remains vulnerable to transparency gaps and elite capture. Senegal cooperation is essential to sustaining the project.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Green-Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and proposed green-hydrogen projects rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export infrastructure. Nouakchott is trying to secure domestic processing and jobs while avoiding excessive exposure to commodity and partner-country risk.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation and Base Politics
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the Diego Garcia military facility and the terms of any long-term foreign presence. The issue tests Port Louis's ability to convert legal and diplomatic gains into effective control.

frictionVectors.title: Port Competition and Strategic Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is balancing Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf commercial interests around ports, logistics, and undersea connectivity. Excessive dependence on any one partner could compromise its autonomy as a maritime services hub.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure investment in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claims. Algeria and the Polisario Front continue to contest this strategy, sustaining regional diplomatic and security friction.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Major port, rail, renewable-energy, and automotive projects depend on European, Gulf, Chinese, and other external financing. Rabat retains strong state direction, but geopolitical competition can create technology, debt, and supply-chain vulnerabilities.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains a Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and external security partners remain central to developing offshore gas and protecting export infrastructure. This limits Maputo's operational autonomy while the state seeks greater revenue and local-content guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten communities, logistics routes, and gas-project timelines. Reliance on foreign and regional forces exposes Mozambique to external leverage over its northern security architecture.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries have intensified competition among international energy firms and raised expectations for stronger state participation. Namibia is seeking favorable fiscal terms and local benefits while avoiding the governance failures associated with oil-dependent economies.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port and Hydrogen Investment
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and green-hydrogen projects could diversify the economy but may create long-term dependence on external capital, technology, and export markets. Windhoek is balancing investment access against control of critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Recontracting
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is pushing to renegotiate or restrict foreign influence over uranium and other strategic resources. This may increase state control, but deteriorating investor confidence and technical constraints threaten production and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Russian and Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The rupture with France and closer ties with Russia and Sahel partners have reduced one form of external dependence while creating another. Insurgent violence and weak regional coordination continue to constrain sovereign control beyond major urban centers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil and Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important to upstream investment, LNG capacity, and technical expertise, even as Nigeria seeks greater domestic ownership and value addition. Theft, sabotage, and regulatory uncertainty continue to weaken state control over petroleum revenues.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, European, and other external financiers are involved in ports, rail, power, and industrial projects. These investments address major infrastructure gaps but can create opaque obligations and reduce Abuja's bargaining room during fiscal stress.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Transit Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral supply chains remains under intense international scrutiny amid allegations that resources from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo move through its territory. Kigali denies wrongdoing and promotes formal processing, but the dispute threatens trade access and diplomatic relations.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda leverages disciplined security forces and foreign partnerships to expand its regional influence, including in eastern Congo and beyond. This generates diplomatic and sanctions exposure while linking national economic interests to a contested security posture.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea offers potential revenue but remains commercially unproven. Limited state capacity increases dependence on foreign technical and financial partners.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure reliance
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China and other partners remain important for infrastructure and public services, narrowing fiscal and strategic room for maneuver.

highlights: Oil and gas production enters a sovereignty test
New leadership presses for contract and debt review

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater national value from offshore projects involving international operators while preserving investor confidence and production stability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large transport and energy projects depend heavily on external finance, while debt constraints limit Dakar's ability to redirect infrastructure policy quickly.

highlights: Blue economy remains the core sovereignty asset
Indian Ocean partnerships diversify strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of maritime access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance Indian, Chinese, European and other security partnerships around port access, surveillance and maritime logistics without becoming strategically overexposed.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries value capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets generate essential licensing revenue, but monitoring capacity and limited domestic processing constrain Seychelles' ability to retain more value.

highlights: Freetown seeks more local value from minerals

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and rutile dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining operations dominate export earnings and infrastructure, leaving public revenue vulnerable to commodity prices, contract terms and operator decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and port facilities link national development to external investors and contractors, creating recurring disputes over transparency, local content and revenue sharing.

highlights: Maritime resources attract competing foreign patrons

frictionVectors.title: Security-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, the African Union and other partners provide critical military, training and infrastructure support, but their competing interests complicate unified national control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas licensing, fisheries access and port interests are entangled with federal-regional disputes and weak regulatory capacity, increasing the risk of contested concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Processing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial control over platinum-group metals, manganese and chrome, but limited domestic refining leaves value capture exposed to foreign capital and downstream processors.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Freight Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and underperforming rail and ports continue to weaken sovereign control over exports, creating openings for private operators and external financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenue remains dependent on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production, transit fees and fiscal stability vulnerable to armed actors and foreign mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and External Capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and opaque oil contracting limit public control of resources, while regional governments and international firms retain leverage over security, logistics and revenue flows.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Networks and Foreign Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to wartime financing, with rival armed networks and external sponsors competing for access to mines, traders and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated transport corridors are strategic lifelines, but conflict, foreign security interests and competing authorities reduce effective national control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Competition
frictionVectors.details: The government is using port, railway and corridor projects to expand regional leverage, but financing and construction partnerships with China, Gulf actors and others create long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and Mining Terms
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is asserting stronger local-content and revenue demands in mining and prospective LNG development, while investors continue pressing for predictable regulations and arbitration protections.

frictionVectors.title: Port Dependence and External Capital
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a regional maritime and transshipment hub increases strategic income, but port operations and associated logistics remain reliant on foreign capital, expertise and commercial networks.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control over phosphate resources, yet limited domestic processing and financing constraints reduce national value capture and preserve exposure to external buyers.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: European financing and migration cooperation give external partners significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress and limited access to affordable capital constrain Tunis's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported energy exposes Tunisia to external price shocks and supply pressure. Delays in renewable investment and regional electricity integration limit near-term sovereignty gains.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP and oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: The oil project offers Uganda future revenue and infrastructure but relies heavily on foreign operators, financing, and export routes. Environmental opposition and sanctions-related pressure continue to raise sovereignty and execution risks.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain important to transport and energy infrastructure. Debt service and project concentration can narrow Kampala's bargaining space even as the government retains formal control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater fiscal returns, local processing, and transparency from international mining companies. However, foreign capital, technology, and marketing networks still dominate the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and multilateral support are easing immediate pressure but impose fiscal and governance constraints. Competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors could improve Lusaka's leverage if managed carefully.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is using export restrictions and local-processing demands to capture more value from lithium and other minerals. Limited domestic capital and technology nevertheless leave major projects dependent on foreign firms, particularly from China.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, currency, and infrastructure constraints
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, monetary instability, and unreliable power and transport raise the cost of sovereign resource development. These pressures push Harare toward opaque bilateral deals and concentrated external partnerships.
